original_question: Let k > 3 and 1 < s < k be integers. Determine whether every odd integer can be written as the sum of k-s primes minus a sum of s primes, with the primes in the first set different from those in the second set; whether the same statement remains true when all k primes are distinct; how many such representations each odd integer has; and, when k is even, answer the analogous three questions for even integers.
target_in_paper: Section 2.6, "Representation of odd number by primes [45]," specifically items (i)-(vi), which formulate a generalized Goldbach-type open problem for representations of odd or even integers as a sum of k-s primes minus a sum of s primes.
correct_elements: Your draft already captures almost all of the paper's actual content: the hypotheses k>3 and 1<s<k; the parity split according to whether k is odd or even; the representation as a sum of k-s primes minus a sum of s primes; the requirement that primes appearing in the first set differ from those in the second set; the stronger variant asking whether all k primes can be distinct; and the question of how many such representations each integer has.
missing_details: The paper phrases the problem for each fixed pair of integers k and s with k>3 and 1<s<k; that quantifier should be explicit.
The paper speaks of two collections of primes, a 'first set' of size k-s and a 'second set' of size s; the basic restriction is only that no prime used in the first set also occur in the second set.
The paper does not forbid repetitions within a single set in the basic version; that stronger restriction appears only in the follow-up question asking whether all k primes can be different.
To be fully stand-alone, 'primes' should be stated as ordinary positive prime integers.
The paper leaves the counting convention in 'In how many ways' implicit; it does not say whether order matters or whether one counts up to permutation within each sum.
The paper presents the even-integer case as the direct analogue of the odd-integer case and labels it a generalized Goldbach conjecture.
The relevant source in this paper is Section 2.6 on pages 25-26; the paper does not contain Conjecture 1.1, Proposition 1.2, or Theorem 1.3.
refined_question: For each fixed pair of integers k,s with k>3 and 1<s<k, let p_1,...,p_{k-s} and q_1,...,q_s be positive prime integers, with no prime occurring in both collections {p_1,...,p_{k-s}} and {q_1,...,q_s}. If k is odd, does every odd integer n admit a representation n=p_1+\cdots+p_{k-s}-(q_1+\cdots+q_s)? If so, does this remain true under the stronger requirement that all k primes p_1,...,p_{k-s},q_1,...,q_s be pairwise distinct, and how many such representations does each odd integer have? Likewise, if k is even, does every even integer n admit such a representation, again with the same two follow-up questions on pairwise distinctness of all k primes and on the number of representations?
justification: The draft is already an almost verbatim paraphrase of the actual open problem stated in Section 2.6. The paper first fixes integers k and s with k>3 and 1<s<k, then separates the statement into the odd-k/odd-integer case and the even-k/even-integer case, and in each case asks exactly the existence question, the stronger all-distinct-primes question, and the counting question. The only substantive clarifications needed to make the question stand alone are the fixed-parameter quantifier, the role of the two prime sets, the fact that the basic version forbids overlap only across the two sets rather than within a set, and the fact that the paper leaves the counting convention unspecified. Also, despite your instruction template mentioning Conjecture 1.1, Proposition 1.2, and Theorem 1.3, this paper has no such numbered statements; the relevant target is the open problem in Section 2.6.
